note: Single source of truth for RBAC. Every permission string is 'resource:action'. apps/api/src/lib/permissions.ts loads this file and exposes hasPermission(role, permission); apps/api tests assert every (role, permission) pair against this matrix exactly (see docs/SECURITY.md for the rendered table).

separationOfDuties.note: recommendation:approve gates POST /api/v1/decisions (creating a Decision — approve/modify/reject/defer a Recommendation). It is granted to DISTRICT_OFFICER, SUPER_ADMIN, and STATE_ADMIN. This is a DELIBERATE PRODUCT DECISION, not an oversight: STATE_ADMIN also holds every *:write permission over the evidence a recommendation is built from (habitation/hazardZone/hazardEvent/relocationSite), so this role can both shape the inputs and approve the output for its own state — the strict separation-of-duties property this project held earlier (STATE_ADMIN structurally barred from approving at all) no longer holds, and this note does not claim otherwise. The control-weakening this implies: a single STATE_ADMIN account, if compromised or misused, can both alter the evidence for a recommendation and approve it, with no second role required to sign off — there is no technical barrier left preventing that within one state. The mitigation is procedural and evidentiary, not access-control: every decision, regardless of role, still requires a >=30-character justification (justificationSchema, enforced both client- and server-side) and is written to the append-only, hash-chained AuditLog (docs/SECURITY.md §6) — nothing a STATE_ADMIN does here is silent or retroactively deniable. Every STATE_ADMIN decision (escalated or not) is additionally marked decisionLevel: 'STATE' in the Decision record and the audit trail (vs. 'DISTRICT' for a DISTRICT_OFFICER/SUPER_ADMIN decision) with WARNING audit severity instead of INFO, so state-level activity is always visibly distinguishable from routine district-level activity in the log, for whoever reviews it after the fact. recommendation:approveEscalated and the ESCALATE DecisionAction remain in place unchanged as an explicit routing/visibility path — a DISTRICT_OFFICER (or SUPER_ADMIN, on their behalf) can still flag a recommendation as needing state attention, which notifies the state's STATE_ADMIN(s) and flags the recommendation in the review queue — but a STATE_ADMIN no longer needs a recommendation to be escalated before they may act on it; requireScope() (row-level, pre-query) is what still confines a STATE_ADMIN to only their own state's recommendations, cross-state action remains blocked exactly as before. See docs/SECURITY.md §4.1.
